title: Impact of Class Size Cap Policy on Reading Scores

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID)

Why: The data contain two groups (treated schools subject to the class-size cap vs. control schools) observed before and after policy implementation. The interaction term `treat_x_post` is the canonical DID estimator.

Key assumption – Parallel Trends: In the absence of the class-size cap, the average reading-score trajectory of treated schools would have moved in parallel with that of control schools. We control for unit (school) fixed effects and period fixed effects to make this assumption more plausible.

Additional assumptions  
• Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spill-overs across schools).  
• No other policy differentially affecting treated schools at the same time.  

## 2. R Code
```r
# -----------------------------
# DID ANALYSIS OF CLASS SIZE CAP
# -----------------------------
# Required packages
if (!requireNamespace("fixest", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("fixest")
if (!requireNamespace("sandwich", quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("sandwich")
if (!requireNamespace("lmtest",   quietly = TRUE)) install.packages("lmtest")

library(fixest)     # fast fixed-effects estimation
library(lmtest)     # coeftest
library(sandwich)   # variance-covariance matrices

# 1. Read data ---------------------------------------------------------------
dat <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s45_data.csv")

# Ensure variables are of correct type
dat$unit_id <- as.factor(dat$unit_id)
dat$period  <- as.factor(dat$period)

# 2. Main DID with two-way fixed effects -------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, 
                  data = dat, 
                  cluster = ~unit_id)          # cluster at school level

cat("\n===== MAIN DID RESULT =====\n")
print(etable(did_main, se = "cluster"), row.names = FALSE)

# Extract point estimate and 95% CI
coef_main   <- coef(did_main)["treat_x_post"]
se_main     <- se(did_main, "cluster")["treat_x_post"]
ci_low_main <- coef_main - 1.96*se_main
ci_hi_main  <- coef_main + 1.96*se_main
cat(sprintf("\nDID estimate (β̂): %.4f  |  95%% CI: [%.4f , %.4f]\n",
            coef_main, ci_low_main, ci_hi_main))

# 3. Robustness checks -------------------------------------------------------

## 3a. Simpler DID without fixed effects
did_simple <- lm(y ~ treat_x_post + treated + post, data = dat)
cat("\n===== SIMPLE DID (no FE) =====\n")
print(coeftest(did_simple, vcov = vcovHC(did_simple, type = "HC1")))

## 3b. Placebo test: use pre-policy observations only -----------------------
# Identify the first post period
post_start <- min(as.numeric(levels(dat$period))[dat$post == 1])

# Keep periods strictly before the policy
dat_pre <- subset(dat, as.numeric(as.character(period)) < post_start)

# Artificially split the pre-period in half to create a “fake” post
pre_periods        <- sort(unique(as.numeric(as.character(dat_pre$period))))
midpoint           <- median(pre_periods)
dat_pre$faux_post  <- as.integer(as.numeric(as.character(dat_pre$period)) > midpoint)
dat_pre$faux_int   <- dat_pre$faux_post * dat_pre$treated

placebo <- feols(y ~ faux_int | unit_id + period, data = dat_pre, cluster = ~unit_id)

cat("\n===== PLACEBO TEST (pre-period only) =====\n")
print(etable(placebo, se = "cluster"), row.names = FALSE)

# 3c. Event-study style leads/lags (if multiple periods) --------------------
# Only run if at least 3 distinct periods exist
if (length(unique(dat$period)) >= 3) {
  # Build relative time indicators
  dat$time_to_treat <- as.numeric(as.character(dat$period)) - post_start
  # Exclude the reference period (-1)
  did_event <- feols(y ~ i(time_to_treat, treated, ref = -1) | unit_id + period,
                     data = dat, cluster = ~unit_id)
  cat("\n===== EVENT-STUDY (leads/lags) =====\n")
  print(summary(did_event, se = "cluster"))
}

# End of script --------------------------------------------------------------
```

## 3. Expected Findings  
Sign: Positive. Smaller classes should allow more individualized instruction and hence boost reading performance, so β̂(treat × post) is expected > 0.

Magnitude: Prior literature often finds gains of 0.10–0.25 standard deviations for substantial class-size reductions in elementary grades. Given that the policy is a cap (likely modest reduction), I expect an effect toward the lower end, roughly +0.12 SD with a 95 % CI of about ±0.10 SD.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Comparative analysis of reading scores before and after the policy in treated and untreated schools.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The class size cap policy resulted in a decrease in reading scores.
